The only solution that 1 perhaps read in this would involve a tremendous additional expenditure of taxpayers dollars which the commission itself does not quantify. Obviously, I would not associate myself with members opposite in agreeing to spending money like that without knowing how much it would be.

speechtext:

came forth in the communiques issued from London and the press reports, on the development of the dispute between Germany and the United States with respect to the handling of the sale of uranium and reactors? Mr. Speaker, I must admire the euphemism that the hon. member uses in saying our position is not that far from that of the United States. He will know, of course, that Canada has taken the lead in this matter. We put on safeguards a considerable period of time before the Americans caught up to us. Naturally, President Carter was stating the view we had already stated many times.
In the debate between President Carter, the German Chancellor and the French president, naturally, the Americans are on the same side as Canada. We all attempted honestly at that summit to find a way out of this difficulty. The hon. member is aware, of course, that we set up a group to establish within 60 days terms of reference for the study which would look at the problem of fuel cycling, to see if there is any way of reaching a compromise on the types of safeguards which are needed and would meet the arguments of both sides.

speakeroldname: Hon. Judd Buchanan (Minister of Public Works):
subsubtopic: EQUITABLE DISTRIBUTION OF JOBS BETWEEN OTTAWA AND HULL-INCREASE IN CROWN-OWNED FACILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since 1969 the government has been implementing a plan for the national capital region with two major objectives: the achievement of a more balanced and equitable distribution of public service jobs between Ottawa and Hull, and an increase in the level of Crown-owned facilities as opposed to leased space. Today 1 would like to announce recent decisions by the government in both these areas and to take the opportunity to recapitulate and clarify the government's position and expectations with regard to development and space utilization in the national capital region.
Particularly since the government's announced policy of slow growth in the public service as part of its over-all restraint program, there has been some concern shown and fears expressed about the effects of government policies on growth and development in the capital. I hope that I can provide a clear picture of our over-all planning for this area and in so doing allay some of the fears and provide a groundwork for planning by all concerned.
At present, the printing and publishing section of the Department of Supply and Services, as well as the Departments of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, Labour and Environment, are located in Hull. As previously announced, we hope that by the end of the current fiscal year most of the Department of Supply and Services, Canadian International Development Agency, the Department of the Secretary of

State, Canadian Radio Telecommunications Commission, and the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs will have moved, or commenced to move, as well. In addition to these relocations, the government has recently decided also to relocate the Solicitor General's department, the Canadian Transport Commission and the Department of Regional Economic Expansion from Ottawa to Hull during this same fiscal year. The Canada Labour Relations Board, Unemployment Insurance Commission, and the Department of Manpower and Immigration are scheduled to move in the 1978-79 period.
The total number of public service jobs involved in these moves is approximately 15,000. With these relocations, the main thrust of the government's relocation policy within the national capital region will have been completed. Except for a number of small units which will be moved to fill up smaller blocks of space in the new buildings, there are no further plans for permanent relocation of government units to office space in Hull for the foreseeable future.
As to the second major objective of the government's national capital region plan, that of increasing the level of Crown-owned facilities as opposed to leased space, there has been considerable revision of our projects for development and construction in light of the government's program of over-all restraint and the related plan for slow growth in the public service over the next few years. I should emphasize that "slow growth" means just that-in the current fiscal year, authorized man-years will be increased by only 0.6 per cent over the 1976-77 level. The continuation of our move toward Crown-owned space and the projected slow growth rate will mean that the government will be returning, on a phased basis, some 4 million square feet of commercially-leased office space to the market over the period to the end of the 1980-81 fiscal year.
Fortunately, the office vacancy rate in the national capital traditionally has been, and is now, substantially lower than in almost any other major Canadian city. Therefore, it appears likely that the building owners, through aggressive application of their entrepreneurial skills, will be able successfully to cope with the admittedly substantial volume of space being released by the federal government.
My departmental officials have been co-operating with the Building Owners and Managers Association-BOMA-to ensure that they have the full, timely information necessary for them to react. Further, we have been informed that the Commercial and Industrial Development Corporation is preparing to mount a vigorous campaign to increase private sector demand for commercial and office accommodation. In addition, the chairman of the National Capital Commission has announced that the NCC intends carefully to study the question of commercial and industrial development with a view to providing whatever assistance it can to encourage greater private sector activity in the national capital. The efforts of these agencies are beginning to show tangible results; recently we were approached by two owners to release space in advance
May 17, 1977

of our original plan, to permit them to accommodate private sector demands.
One of our main concerns in attempting to alleviate the impact of these necessary inventory adjustments has been for the smaller shop and restaurant owners, which both support the occupants of the buildings we lease and, to some extent, rely upon their trade to stay in business. Accordingly, we are negotiating with the building owners, through BOMA, and with the downtown merchants, in an attempt to arrive at an arrangement which will permit us evenly to spread the effects across our rental inventory. If we are successful in securing the full co-operation of building owners, it should be possible to ensure that no specific area is critically damaged or required to absorb an inequitable share of the burden.
In order further to ease the transition, the government is taking advantage of this period of consolidation to demolish over 2 million square feet of old, inefficient space in temporary or obsolescent buildings throughout the city of Ottawa over the next two years. I should point out that even after these inventory adjustments the government will continue lease or lease-purchase arrangements for 7.7 million square feet of office space in the national capital region: 2.3 million square feet on the Quebec side, and 5.4 million square feet on the Ontario side. Incidentally, some concern has been expressed recently about the impact of income tax deductions on residents of Ontario working in Quebec. This is a concern, of course, not only for federal civil servants residing in Ontario whose departments are relocated in Hull, but also for some employees in the private sector. I am happy to report that my colleague, the Minister of National Revenue, will describe a solution to this problem in a separate announcement.
I am pleased to confirm, also, that the agreement signed in 1975 by representatives of the Outaouais Regional Community Transit Commission, the Ottawa-Carleton Regional Transit Commission and the NCC is currently being reviewed. Negotiations between the parties are expected to lead to a similar agreement providing passengers with a choice of interchangeable services to and from both sides of the Ottawa River, augmented as necessary to meet the demand.
Although the restraint program has restricted Crown construction in the Ottawa area, the government is concerned that the core of the city of Ottawa continue to be vital and thriving. In particular, the government has long favoured the development of the Rideau Centre, a proposed major complex on an 8 1 /2-acre tract of federal land on the east side of the Rideau Canal. The development of this area has had wide support and it is felt would make a substantial contribution to the revitalization of the whole Rideau core area. The government will shortly be publicly inviting proposals for development of the centre. The first stage will enable potential developers to express their interest and demonstrate their capacity to undertake such a venture. As originally planned, this centre would feature a major hotel, a major department store and other retail outlets and some 700,000 square feet of office space, much of which would be occupied by the federal government.
Public Service
In view of the present situation, it has been decided not to include office space in the Rideau Centre development proposal call on federal land. Nevertheless, the government has decided to move ahead with the other aspects of the centre in the belief that this will have a beneficial over-all effect on the Rideau core and will be welcomed by the Ottawa business community.
I hope the?" comments will help to clarify the government's plans for development in the national capital region in the medium-term future. There is no question that insofar as the federal government is concerned we shall be going through a period of consolidation rather than the fairly rapid growth we have experienced over the past few years. However, over-all there will continue to be some growth in the NCR as a whole and, of course, the municipalities in the area will continue vigorously to pursue alternative courses leading to a more diversified industrial and commercial life for the region.
I am sure hon. members are also interested in the government's plans to move government units from the national capital region to other parts of the country. This is a complex issue, involving a number of difficult assessments and choices. The government has already made some announcements on its plans in this regard but is not in a position to make a comprehensive statement at the present time. It hopes to do so in the next few weeks. I wish to emphasize, however, that there will be no overlap between these moves to Hull and decentralization outside of the national capital, with the minor exception of a few smaller units already announced, involving approximately 450 jobs in all.

Under the agreement, the Quebec government will reduce income tax for federal employees. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: EQUITABLE DISTRIBUTION OF JOBS BETWEEN OTTAWA AND HULL-INCREASE IN CROWN-OWNED FACILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is an interesting day in the life of the national capital area. We are now seeing the government attempting to justify, on the backs of the Public Service of Canada, a proposal which was made to develop what I call Fort Fullerton on the other side of the Ottawa river, a decision that was reached without any forethought or consultation whatsoever.
If I may deal with the statement of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Buchanan), using his language, this is an attempt to justify a decision which was made without any planning or consultation with anyone. I refer to the development of those buildings on the other side of the Ottawa river. The buildings are there; anyone can see them if they look across the river. They stand there at great public expense, and I think it is important that the people of Canada know just how little planning, discussion and consultation went into the decision to put them there.
I am not speaking from lack of knowledge. 1 am speaking from information that was given to me by the government in an answer to a question which I put on the order paper on November 19, 1976. It is of interest to note that there was so little planning, so little digging and so little to look for that the government was uncharacteristically quick in answering that question on November 22, 1976. The question asked whether a task force on relocation of departments and agencies to Hull has been formed and, if so who are the members, what are the terms of reference, has it begun to function, on what date is a report expected, and will it be tabled in the House or published as a white paper? To that question the answer was no. So some time between November of last year and today's announcement somebody scurried around and found some departments which they could move to Hull. If making an announcement in this way within that short period of time is not an example of lack of co-ordination, then 1 do not know what is, Mr. Speaker.
As for development of the area itself, I put certain questions on the order paper on November 19. For example, No. 1,141 has never been answered, though it is being partly answered today. I asked in the fourth part of the question:
What consultation has been undertaken with Hull to determine the best means of maximizing benefits and minimizing harmful effects on the city (b) what consultation has taken place with the city of Ottawa to minimize possible harmful effects on the city?
The minister's statement did not deal with this, which means that there has been no consultation whatever. If the statement of the Minister of Public Works marks a failure in anything- and I say this with regret and without any reprobation of the hon. member himself-it marks a failure in the efforts of the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis), the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Poulin) and the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), who within their caucus, as it is described by the Minister of National Revenue (Miss

Begin), have tried to persuade the government to use its head and to think about what it is doing.
The justification for a ministry of the public service to look after the interest of the public servants of Canada has been put forward time and time again by the hon. member for Ottawa West. In terms of consultation with the corporation of the city of Ottawa, the regional municipality of Ottawa-Carleton and all the municipalities around, on a matter that affects them gravely, the government has admitted today that there has been none whatsoever. This step has been taken to fill buildings on the other side of the river which were constructed without any study at all being made. They are a figment of some bureaucratic mind; they are standing there today and they must be filled. That is the situation we are in in the national capital today. In other words, it is a Ruby Goldberg day in the national capital.
Another matter which concerns me, regarding which members of the House have tried to deal, is the matter of getting co-ordination between the government's plan to decentralize the public service, on the one hand, and relocation of the public service to Hull, on the other hand. This statement, on its face, is an indication that this step has been taken separate and apart from decentralization. Relocation is not considered as part and parcel of decentralization in terms of areas affected. That is an admission of failure. It is dereliction of duty on the part of the government, not simply on the part of the Minister of Public Works who is only the fellow who has to carry the can today. This lack of co-ordination between decentralization and relocation reminds me, quite frankly, of an octopus in heat, and I think it is about time somebody said so.
Have any studies been made of this proposal for the growth and development of the national capital? None whatsoever. How can we believe the well-intentioned Minister of Public Works when he says that only 15,000 public servants will be transferred to Hull? Do you remember, Mr. Speaker, the bilingualism program in this city? It started out first as a policy involving 25,000 people. Then there was a little leak out of the government to the effect that it would be double that and, by golly, the government admitted that 53,000 would be affected. Now we are up to 65,000 positions and there is no indication that that figure is going to be lessened. If the Minister of National Revenue, who is interjecting, will be patient, what I am saying is that the disease of this government is that its figures mean nothing since there are no studies upon which those statistics are based.
Who is going to carry the freight for a policy which has been made without consultation with the city of Ottawa, the regional municipality and the municipalities around? Who but the old entrepreneurial skills of the private sector? The entrepreneurial skills of the private sector in the national capital area in a time of slow growth are going to be tested like they have never been tested before. If there is any meaning to the statement by the chairman of the National Capital Commission with respect to providing some help to develop the private sector and increase employment, then it had better become apparent quickly. There had better be some flesh put on the
May 17, 1977

skeleton, instead of the pious statement which the minister made to the House today.
I laughed out loud when the minister expressed concern for the small shop and restaurant owners and stated how the government was going to rationalize the position of small shop and restaurant owners in the city of Ottawa who had developed on the basis of one particular scheme of development and who now find the rug pulled out from under them by a government which has about as much co-ordination as the octopus that I have mentioned. I am sure the hon. member for Ottawa Centre and the hon. member for Ottawa West-and I bet that if he were here, the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier would nod his head, too-have received letter after letter, as I have, from members of the business community in Ottawa asking why they are not being consulted and being told what the government is doing. I suggest it would be uncharacteristic of the government ever to consult. If they will not consult with their own public service unions, and if they will not give advance notice to them of decentralization, how could we ever expect them to consult with such forms of life, in their consideration, as smaller shop and restaurant owners in the national capital area? They even admit in the statement that damage is going to occur. They say on page 3 of the statement that there is going to be something less than critical damage. Well, that is a comfort. They are going to do their best to deal with that. In the statement there is no rationalization of transportation problems.
1 am delighted to see the government has announced, for the fifth time-twice in the 1972 election, twice in the 1974 election, and today-that we are going to proceed with the Rideau Centre. That is a wonderful thing. But I want to warn the proponents of the Rideau Centre that, like bilingualism and the designation of bilingual jobs which has escalated, the promise with respect to the Rideau Centre is de-escalating. We were going to start with a big project, and now it is going down and down. I wager there will be a sixth announcement in the future concerning the development of the Rideau Centre in Ottawa.
Referring to the whole business of relocation, I remind the government the only place within the national capital area is in the city of Hull, and the official plans for the townships of Nepean, Goulbourn, Osgoode and Rideau, and the whole aspect of the regional government plan in this area asks for government installations in those areas as part of relocation projects. Why the government continues to place more and more square footage of office space in one area of the national capital, and denies that kind of development to the other areas, 1 leave that to hon. members to speculate about. That demand is there. That is a demand that ought to be remembered, and not forgotten, as it has been forgotten by this government.
The statement of the Minister of Public Works is a dreadful one for the national capital area. We have come to this point without consultation with the public service unions, the municipalities involved, and without any meaningful plans to assist
Public Service
the private sectors. Lip service is given to that in this statement. This point has been reached without any meaningful plans with respect to transportation, and without settling the matter of sewage treatment on one side of the Ottawa River. Making these announcements is further indication of lack of co-ordination which has afflicted this ministry since 1969.

I am sure the business community of Ottawa made known their points of view. If they had been consulted and listened to, there would be nothing in Hull. It is parliament which makes the decisions, not the business community of Ottawa. I should like to talk about the business community of Ottawa and the kind of decisions they have made for this city in the past.
I am delighted the National Capital Commission owns the land which will be the future site of the Rideau Centre. Those 8% acres will not be built on, if the National Capital Commission has anything to say about it, in a way that will overshadow the parliament buildings. Those acres will not be built on in a way which will allow for the maximum amount of assessment regardless of the consequences to Parliament Hill. Unfortunately, the policy of the city of Ottawa in the past has been virtually to laugh at the attitude of the National Capital Commission in regard to height restriction: the greater the height, the greater the assessment, so let them go as high as they like, not matter what it does to Parliament Hill! To build in Hull and to move some 15,000 public servants there will create a number of problems. The Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin) has taken steps to correct some of those problems. Over the years Ottawa has been getting the industrial and commercial assessments in many cases, and Hull has been the bedroom town with all that is involved in terms of a tax base. Some of that is going to be redressed by this move. It is long overdue that we should redress this imbalance.
My hon. friend who spoke on behalf of the Conservative party worries about the fact there has been no planning. He is right. There was probably no planning involved here. At some point I would like to question the minister to find out what Mr. Coolican's attitude has been to this kind of trade-off. speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-55, to amend the Customs Tariff (No. 2), be read the second time and referred to committee of the whole.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to give effect to the amendments to the Customs Tariff which were proposed in the budget of March 31, 1977. The amendments fall into three broad categories: first, those required to continue in force for another year the temporary tariff reductions which would otherwise have expired on June 30, 1977; second, those designed to implement certain concessions for products of interest to the developing countries which we have agreed to make in the context of the discussions in Geneva on multilateral trade negotiations; and third, a number of miscellaneous amendments, including the withdrawal of the British preferential tariff rate on certain machinery imported from Britain and Ireland.
First let me deal with the question of temporary reductions. The principal provisions of the bill, in clause 3 and schedule II, provide for the extension until June 30, 1978, of a large number of temporary tariff reductions on consumer goods which were originally introduced as an anti-inflation measure in the budget of February 19, 1973. The value of imports affected is about $1.4 billion in terms of 1976 trade. About $400 million of this is in the food sector. Other products covered by the package include drugs and pharmaceuticals, kitchen and dinnerware, hand tools, photographic equipment and sporting goods.
The coverage of the package as of July 1, 1977, will differ in three respects from that now in effect. First, the reduced rates of duty on lighting fixtures are being allowed to expire on June 30 because of the difficulties domestic manufacturers have had in competing against imports. Second, the duty on refined sugar is being increased by one-fifth of a cent per pound to provide refiners with the net amount of protection recommended by the Tariff Board when it reviewed the tariffs on sugar several years ago. I should point out, however, that the new rates of duty on refined sugar are still below those which were in effect prior to the 1973 budget. All we are doing is restoring them to the levels which were in effect between February, 1973, and November, 1974. Third, tariff reductions on several tropical products which were previously part of the temporary measure are being continued in force on a permanent basis pursuant to the provisions in the bill relating to concessions for developing countries.
With respect to concessions to developing countries, the second category, the proposed tariff reductions on products of special interest to developing countries have been discussed with these countries in the "tropical products group" which

May 17, 1977
Customs Tariff
was set up in the framework of the multilateral trade negotiations. This group was established to see if something could be done on a priority basis, before the end of the negotiations as a whole, to improve the export earnings and balance of trade of the developing countries.
The Canadian concessions are of two kinds. First, we have added a number of products to the list of goods that are eligible for the general preferential tariff, which applies only to imports from developing countries. Second, we have also reduced or removed the permanent most favoured nation tariff on a number of "tropical products" which are produced mainly in developing countries. The concessions which are being implemented through changes in the general preferential tariff are provided for in clause 2 and schedule I of the bill, while those being implemented on a most favoured nation basis are provided for in clause 4 and schedule III. These proposed changes will affect about $100 million of imports from developing countries.
The third category, as I indicated, is with regard to some miscellaneous tariff charges. As I have indicated, the most important amendment in the miscellaneous group-clauses 5 and 6 and schedules IV and V-is the proposal to make certain machinery and related equipment from Britain and Ireland subject to the 15 per cent most favoured nation rate rather than the 2'h per cent British preferential rate. This amendment flows from the study of the tariffs on machinery from Britain and Ireland which I announced in the budget of 1976.
This study was initiated as a result of representations from Canadian manufacturers that imports of British machinery at the preferential rate were adversely affecting production in Canada. Canada, of course, is no longer required to accord preferential tariff treatment to imports from Britain and Ireland since they withdrew preferences on our exports when they joined the European Economic Community.
On the basis of our review to date, we concluded that the Canadian manufacturers of the nine categories of machinery which are being added to the provisions of tariff item 42701-1 had made a case for withdrawal of the preferential rate at this time. When machinery in these categories is not available from Canadian sources, the duty can be remitted under the machinery program. The Department of Finance will continue to monitor the situation with respect to imports of other kinds of machinery from Britain and Ireland. The bill also provides authority for an increase of 2'h percentage points in the duties on polypropylene resin and on certain products made from this resin. Canadian production of the resin will come onstream in the near future.
The schedule of miscellaneous amendments also provides for continuation of duty-free entry on a temporary basis for various petroleum products and for aircraft. Other amendments are designed to resolve certain problems which have come to light. A number of these are of a relieving nature; for example, the provisions which will accord free entry to cameras and other equipment for the production of films. On the other hand, the $7,500 value limit on individual articles which

may be brought back by Canadians duty and tax free after a period of residence abroad is designed to prevent abuse of existing duty and tax free provisions.
That, Mr. Speaker, is a general review of the items involved. In committee of the whole I will, of course, be glad to deal with any specific questions.

Mr. Speaker, this is one of the non-items arising out of a very bland budget. We received some amendments to Customs Tariffs in the past which were really much more noticeable or had a much higher profile from a policy point of view. For example, in schedule II there is an extension of two years of a three-year program of tropical fruits and certain things. I was very struck by the first item in 705-2, the admission of frogs legs free into Canada.
It may be that some people consider that a Customs Tariff is a very dry-bones subject and has no humour in it. I do not want to take too much time on this particular bill. I have already mentioned frogs legs in schedule I on page 5. The same schedule, on page 6, refers to fruits, dried, desiccated, evaporated or dehydrated; namely, breadfruit, guavas, litchis, mangoes, mangosteens, pineapples and soursop. What is sour-sop? I am sure even the minister does not know that one. Item 10525-5 takes you through mangosteens, soursop and mangoes, including mango chutney, which is a particular delicacy for my colleague, the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse). He really loves mango chutney and will be quite happy with that.
On these particular points I would like to know from the minister if, as a result of the three years special tariff on these tropical fruits and part of the extension of freedom of the Canadian market to developing countries outside of the general preferential tariff, there has been any movement of goods into the country. Do items such as these, where we now have free entry, mean anything? Is there a meaningful movement into the country-of a particularly sophisticated kind, I will admit-of such items as 13300-2, caviar being prepared from sturgeon roe, being admitted free? There are others.
One I find most intriguing is item 52306-1, page 8, schedule I. I wonder why this particular item is now being admitted free. This has to with industrial shop towels, hemmed but not bleached or dyed except for identification markings. It lists the various sizes. Are there not, within the Canadian textile industry, ample facilities to produce these industrial shop towels at a price where foreign imports could not be used to drive down prices, that is, costs in the industrial field; or is it in response to representations from any particular country or countries that this is something they would like to sell us in reasonable quantities in exchange for their purchase of other Canadian goods? I think we should have an explanation.
I do not want to belabour this bill. A good deal was said about the principles of it as we debated the tax changes and tariff changes during the budget debate. Several of my colleagues are going to question certain parts as their particular areas may be most severely affected by some of these proposals. I was a little surprised that the minister did not speak
May 17, 1977

about what he felt was the progress on the present GATT talks at Geneva out of the Tokyo round. I was disappointed he did not tell us what progress the government had made in responding to the serious representations made by members on this side of the House as well as by some of the provincial premiers whose full intention it is to insist upon consultation with the provinces with respect to tariff changes. It seems to me that not only do they have a point, but that they have an indisputable case. There is no question but that the premiers have full jurisdiction with regard to development within their own provinces, and unilateral action on the part of the government of Canada in the course of these negotiations, without disclosing what is being acquired and what is being given away, is simply not good enough. A province might very well find that its industrial policy had been thoroughly undermined.
I have mentioned before the implementation of certain features of the Kennedy round having to do with the heavy chemical producing industry across the country. That industry was hard pressed, to start with, as a result of the Kennedy round negotiations. Indeed, it seemed to me that in many instances the concessions made in the field of industrial chemicals were regarded as among the throw-away items. The changes which were to be implemented were to be placed on a five-year basis. But less than two years after the conclusion of the Kennedy round the then minister of finance, Mr. Benson, suddenly telescoped all the remaining reductions into one year. The result was, of course, disastrous for the chemical industry.
I, for one, and my colleagues from Alberta as well, will be very reluctant to accept any concessions made at the GATT negotiations which will further seriously affect the developing industrial chemical industry in Alberta. I suppose that in toto it is the biggest such complex in the country. The problems it faces are already tough enough, in the face of world competition. There is the distance from markets, for example. A considerable element of transportation cost is involved before getting to offshore.
The situation is tough. These firms are finding it hard to meet competition in the domestic market on the basis that a world-scale plant produces 8 per cent to 10 per cent, so perhaps a little more of that plant's capacity will satisfy the Canadian market. So I want to know, as do my colleagues, to what degree is there consultation? By this I mean active consultation, not a telephone call the night before a decision is taken. I mean actual participation on the negotiating teams of representatives of industry and the provincial governments.
In this respect I think we should seek to emulate our United States counterparts who, incidentally, are very successful in these tariff negotiations. They take their people into their confidence and are quite open about what they want to do. Somehow or other, we seem to believe in playing our cards very close to the vest; we think everything ought to be kept under the shell, obliging our own people to guess where the pea is hidden.

I see the minister making notes in readiness to reply. Several of my hon. friends have brief comments to make. We do not believe there should be a very extensive debate over this bill, and if the minister is forthcoming in his answers I do not doubt we shall make good progress with this measure. Subject to my commitments on the estimates committee which is dealing with the Department of National Revenue this evening, I hope we can progress rapidly in dealing with Bill C-54.
Mr. Speaker, I rise simply to say that we are quite prepared to have the bill go into committee of the whole forthwith.

Mr. Speaker,
1 welcome the opportunity to debate this bill. We very seldom have an opportunity to talk in this House on the important subject of Customs Tariffs, but it is a very important subject to Canadian industry. This is an opportunity which usually comes to us after a budget. We get these changes in Customs Tariffs usually involving the lowering of tariffs or else keeping the status quo. Very seldom, if ever, are any of the tariffs raised in the rush by the government to get into a free trade situation as quickly as possible.
Today, many segments of industry in Canada are facing hard times. 1 think particularly of small manufacturing businesses and related enterprises. I think, for example, of firms manufacturing recreational vehicles, motor homes and mobile homes. Times are hard for the boat manufacturers, the electronics industry, the textile industry and the shoe manufacturing industry. Only recently we were hearing noises from the manufacturers of parts for automobiles. Then, as always, there is the case of farm products. These industries are finding it increasingly hard to compete with imports, and the tariff structure, or lack of it, is one factor which makes it difficult for them to do so.
The manufacture of recreational vehicles and mobile homes is quite extensive in my riding. It is important to large numbers of my constituents. Representations have been made to the minister over the past few months with regard to the tariff imposed on the component parts used in the manufacture of these vehicles. The tariff was lowered to 15 per cent a few years ago, but the charge on most of the parts which are not manufactured in Canada and would have to be imported is between 17'/2 per cent and 20 per cent. This means that if a recreational vehicle is manufactured in the United States, for instance, and shipped into Canada, the component parts in that vehicle are charged at only 15 per cent. However, if a manufacturer in Canada goes to the United States and buys the parts there, he is obliged to pay between M'A per cent and 20 per cent, which is really not fair trade. It makes it difficult for the Canadian manufacturer to compete. The whole tariff field is complex and difficult to understand.
Quite often when tariff changes are made there is a chain of reaction against manufacturers or industry in Canada. Unfortunately, manufacturers of recreational homes are considering

May 17, 1977
Customs Tariff
moving from Canada to the United States, as are other industries today. This is a situation we should not allow to happen. There is very high unemployment in Canada and we are looking for ways and means of employing people, yet the situation is such that industries are caused to move from Canada because it is more profitable for them to export their products back to Canada from some other country.
We cannot have it both ways, Mr. Speaker. If we are to do something to assist major industry and business in Canada, we must take a good, hard look at the situation and make sure that we do not inhibit manufacturers from producing their goods in Canada. We need employment. We cannot export people along with our manufacturers, yet we make it very easy for manufacturers simply to pick up and move out, make a profit in another country and send their products back here.
The electronics industry is in the same situation today as textiles and farm products. Although this is not the entire fault of tariffs, quite a lot of the blame is. Most of the problem has to do with trade and trading and bringing imports into Canada, and this is where the tariff structure comes in. People in the electronics industry talk about fair trade, just as do the people who produce farm products, and they see very many areas where we do not have fair trade. Our exports have to meet trade barriers, while we make it very easy to import into Canada.
Let me now come to my favourite topic, farm products. Bill C-55 deals with many farm products and continues temporary tariff reductions which were made previously. These reductions apply to products such as asparagus, beets, carrots and tomato juice-products that we should encourage Canadians to grow. Quite a few people in Canada argue that if we can get these products cheaper somewhere else, then let us import them and not worry about the Canadian farmer. But that is not the way to build this nation; we cannot build the nation with that kind of philosophy.
These same people are telling us to make sure that we do not pave any more farmland. I agree with them, because in time we are going to need all the farmland we can get. That is why we must ensure that our farmers get the chance to make a decent living. I have quite often heard Liberal governments say we should stabilize farming, that we should have stabilization programs, but in the long run I do not believe that stabilization programs are necessarily the best way to preserve agriculture. What we also need is proper protection in our tariff structure.
A couple of weeks ago the report of the Tariff Board respecting fresh and processed fruits and vegetables was laid on the table. I do not know when we will have a chance to discuss the report in the House, if ever. Seldom do we get the opportunity to discuss anything to do with tariffs in this House. We have the GATT round and the Kennedy round, and pretty well such decisions are made by the bureaucracy and approved by cabinet. Such matters are not really discussed in the House of Commons where the opposition has a chance to say something.
The Tariff Board report on fruits and vegetables is a very good one and certainly does not go along the lines of the action

taken by the Minister of Finance over the last few years of reducing tariffs on farm products. The fruits and vegetables industry has done a terrific job of informing the Tariff Board about what is going on, and I certainly hope the board's recommendations will quickly be acted upon. Llowever, we do not know what route is going to be taken to make these recommendations law and to incorporate them in the tariff provisions, if that is what is going to be done by cabinet. As I say, we do not get an opportunity to discuss the matter, which in my opinion is undesirable.
I will not take up any more time of the House except to say that, so far as the general over-all philosophy of free and fair trade is concerned, I think there should be a more complete review of the whole tariff structure so that we do not find certain tariffs penalizing producers or manufacturers in Canada. I have a few questions I should like to ask, but 1 will save them for when we get into committee of the whole.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few comments to make on Bill C-55. At the outset I should like to echo the words of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) who underlined the importance of tariff negotiations so far as Alberta is concerned, particularly with regard to agricultural and petrochemical products. These are very important to the industrial capacity of the province of Alberta, a fact which I should like to impress upon the minister. I would like to deal today with three industries which are of grave importance to the prairies and western Canada. They are the pork industry, the beef industry and the rapeseed industry. I would like to deal with them in that order as far as tariffs are concerned.
On February 20, 1973, the tariff on canned pork was substantially reduced. This bill calls for a continuation of that reduction. This is despite the fact that the hog industry in western Canada is on the verge of collapse. The industry is in trouble, and low tariff rates have only served to aggravate the problem. In 1971, Alberta produced 2,015,000 hogs. By 1975, this figure had been slashed almost in half to a total production of only 1,242,000 hogs. Many pork packing plants across Alberta have been shut down and the remaining operations are running at 35 per cent to 50 per cent of their capacity.
Tariff rates have not been the sole, nor even the major reason, for the decline of the hog industry in western Canada. Most of these problems relate to the problem of freight rates whereby it is cheaper to ship 800 pounds of barley to eastern Canada to raise one hog than it is to raise a hog in western Canada and ship the meat out to eastern markets. It would be a favour to western markets if the tariff was increased to an adequate proportion in order to eliminate some of the import-export anomalies we see.
In 1975, $77 million worth of pork was imported into Canada. By 1976, this had increased to $144 million worth of pork shipped into this country. At the same time, we are only exporting some $93 million. You can see the effect this is having. We have doubled our imports of pork products into
May 17, 1977

Canada within one year, and our exports have remained virtually the same or have dropped slightly.
1 would like to deal for a moment with the continuation of low tariffs on vegetable oils. The highlights of this plight of the industry in the west is that the oilseed crushing industry is not going ahead at the pace it should be. 1 know of one or two plants in western Canada which are ready to start building if they could get the proper concessions as far as tariffs and freight rates are concerned. Without getting into the problem of freight rates, because I know that does not come under the jurisdiction of this bill, I would like to put before the House the supposition that if we cannot get the proper freight rate structure for the oilseed crushing plants in western Canada, maybe the answer is in a proper tariff structure.
At present it is cheaper for eastern Canada to import their vegetable oils for use in the kitchens than it is to bring in western crushed oilseed. This, of course, is because of the freight rate structure. If we could get a proper tariff structure on the importation of vegetable oils, this would provide the distinct advantage which is needed until the minister stops procrastinating on the freight rate structure and allows us to bring rapeseed oil and rapeseed meal into eastern Canada at the rate at which we are now shipping uncrushed rapeseed.
My last representation has to do with western Canada's beef industry. The item I want to refer to is the ad valorem duty which is being charged by the United States. It ranges from 7.5 per cent to 10 per cent on all boxed beef which is going into the United States. As a producer of beef in western Canada, I have to take that steer or heifer to a packing plant, have it slaughtered and put into a boxed condition ready to be shipped to the United States market directly into a store or a restaurant. I am being charged 7.5 per cent to 10 per cent ad valorem duty by the American government to send that boxed beef to the United States.
At the same time, a producer in the United States doing the same thing is allowed to bring his beef into Canada at a mere three cents per pound, which is a standard rate Canadians and Americans pay at the border for any carcass beef that crosses. This is a direct discrimination against the western beef farmer in processing his product in the packing plant. This is something we should look at very closely.
I am not advocating we should put on a 7.5 per cent to 10 per cent ad valorem duty here in Canada to offset what they are doing to the beef industry in the United States. I am advocating we should be entering into negotiations with the United States government to eliminate that discriminatory factor and allow it to cross the border at the three-cent tariff which is applied to American beef coming into Canada. All we are asking for is the same treatment. This has been going on for at least ten years, if not longer. In order to create more jobs in the packing industry in western Canada, it is absolutely essential, as we move more and more to the boxed beef trade for the restaurant market, to get the same treatment. Over a third of our meals are now eaten in restaurants, which is increasing rapidly to the point where in the next three or four years half of our meals will be eaten outside the home.
Customs Tariff
1 would like to ask the minister one question in the area of small business. I cannot understand why a tariff is charged on machinery coming into this country which we are not capable of producing. To give an example of this, an industry in my riding is setting up a plant to produce plastic boxes for stores. They required a printing press to print on those plastic boxes. They were unable to find a printing press in Canada and found out that such a printing press could not be produced. Thus, they had to go outside Canada to buy the press. It cost some $300,000, and they were charged a 15 per cent tariff. That is a substantial amount of money to a small business which is scratching to get started and is faced with a sum of money like that which has to be paid to the federal government. That is unfair and is something we should look at. If we are not capable of producing that machinery in Canada, then there should be no tariff on its crossing the border.
In conclusion, it is a good practice to have no tariff on tropical produce. It is more sensible to allow that produce in free, than shipping hundreds of thousands of dollars of Canadian taxpayers' money to those countries in order to help them out with their balance of trade payments.

Mr. Speaker, to begin with, I would like to compliment the minister on one inclusion in the tariff. I am referring to item No. 46218-1 which is a tariff item that relates to the film animation industry. This is a relatively new industry in Canada. It is encouraging to see they will be able to bring related machinery into the country duty-free in at least two areas, except for the third item which is the most favoured nation column. I want to thank the minister for that. It is necessary this new industry be supported in that way and I compliment the government for recognizing this need.
Having said that, I want to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Whittaker). The policy of the government is contradictory in this area because, on the one hand, the government has created a tariff classification in order to help new industry, but on the other hand industry which is already established in Canada is having a hard time making a go of it.
I refer specifically to the leisure craft industry which produces campers and trailers. In my riding of Surrey-White Rock there is a large leisure vehicle industry, and because of rising taxes at all levels of government, rising labour costs and rising material costs, the industry cannot make it any longer in Canada. It is moving to the state of Washington. It is going to continue manufacturing leisure vehicles there. Canada can be serviced from the state of Washington better than if the industry is operating within Canada. Something must be rotten in the state of Denmark when a wholly-owned Canadian industry which was born in Canada and which has been operating in Canada for a couple of decades has to move to the United States to service Canada. It is time we took a new look at our taxation structure in order to help industries which are trying to make a go of it.

May 17, 1977
Customs Tariff
1 would like to bring to the attention of the minister just one item. I raised this the last time there was a budget debate. It relates to marksmen, whether they are target shooters, skeet shooters, or whatever. The Canadian industry has stopped making components for ammunition; that is, shells, cartridges and shot. All those items are no longer manufactured in Canada. All you can get is the completely assembled bullet, shell, or whatever it is called, which is manufactured in Quebec. There are many people in British Columbia who are members of gun clubs and who do not want to pay the high, assembled price of those components.
Over and over again in schedule IV of the tariff we find the phrase "those items not made in Canada". I would like to ask the minister why it is not possible for this item to be declared duty-free so that people who see assembling these bullets as part of their hobby can be accommodated. Why can they not bring the component parts from the United States or from other countries and assemble them themselves? Why should they have to pay up to 12 times as much for the assembled item, when they could get it in its component parts and have the pleasure of assembling the bullets themselves, as well'as saving all that money?
I know the minister will argue that this is a revenue-producing item, but if that is the case, why not for all these items? Why pick on this one item? I would like to have a clear answer from the minister as to why the tariff is on this one simple item which is important to target shooters and skeet shooters. These people purchase in large volume, and this tariff makes it very difficult for them to practice their hobby as much as they would wish. Why has the minister not included that in the tariff arrangements for this year? That is one item about which I would like to have a clear and concise answer from the minister.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make a few comments to show that governments sometimes admit they make mistakes, and sometimes they even take action to correct them. On December 13, 1976, during a debate on scientific research relating to a bill on government organization with regard to scientific activities, I made reference to tariff item 69605-1 which is a tariff item dealing with scientific apparatus including scientific preparations used in teaching, in research and in medical diagnoses, these items being equipment and chemicals of various types.
Over the past five years there has been a severe erosion in Canada in the area of scientific research and medical research-all kinds of research, as a matter of fact-because of a policy of this government which suggests that very much research is not really necessary in this country because we can simply import it and thereby get it at a lower cost. The tariff item to which 1 am referring was changed a couple of years ago. These items were free of tariff originally, but for some strange reason somebody in the government got the idea that a tariff should be applied. The result of that was to increase the hardship for research people in Canada because the cost of research went up by 6 per cent to 10 per cent. Following many vigorous representations by researchers from across the coun-
[Mr. Friesen.1
try and by hon. members from this side of the House I am pleased to note that the government has now seen the folly of its ways and has again proposed in this bill to abolish the tariff on these items.
I wanted to make these few comments in order to show the House of Commons, the country and the world that members of the opposition are not afraid to say something complimentary about the government when it is deserved. I must emphasize, however, that I am speaking strictly about one specific tariff item. There are many others on which action could have been taken which has not been taken. The government should be severely castigated for this. However, on this particular item I think the correct action has been taken.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Roy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PERMIT OBJECTIONS BY CITIZENS TO CHANGE OF RAIL LINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am again pleased to be able to participate in this discussion on Bill C-207 to amend section 119 of the Railway Act. As I indicated in my comments during second reading on November 23, 1976, and again on April 25, 1977, when this bill was carefully examined by the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, this is a bill which addresses itself to increasing public information and awareness by requiring railroad companies to provide four weeks' public notice of plans to change or expand railway tracks in residential areas. This is an important step in making the railways more responsible and considerate of the public they serve. In this respect, I am sure that all hon. members recognize the need for adoption of this legislation.
During detailed study of this bill in committee 1 moved an amendment which was unanimously adopted by the committee. The amendment in no sense changed the major thrust of this private member's bill. Rather, it broadened the scope of the bill to include not only residences but also commercial and public buildings located within a distance of 1,000 feet of the planned railway facilities. The amendment also provided for the Canadian Transport Commission to exercise practical discretion in administering the act.
The railways are not required to advise local citizens when existing facilities are to be deviated, changed, expanded or otherwise, when those fall within the scope of section 119. The value of Bill C-207 to the Railway Act is reflected by the unanimous and positive reception which the bill received on second reading and in committee. I urge that this bill again receive the unanimous support of all hon. members. I should like to thank all hon. members who participated in the debate on this legislation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may 1 say a few words, in reply to comments made this afternoon. I began to say this afternoon, subsequent to the comment made by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) with respect to consultation, that my predecessor over two years ago invited the provinces to make submissions with regard to Canada's position at the Tokyo Round of tariff negotiations, and a few provinces have responded to that by indicating their positions. Many more have not. I would have to say that 1 would welcome provincial participation on this question. Indeed, I would welcome the participation of the provinces at a meeting of finance ministers, at which we could collectively address ourselves to some of the issues involved. Last, but not least, I would welcome the provinces giving some priority to considering what they would be prepared to pay in terms of trade-offs in order to get tariff reductions abroad, and to considering their objectives for developing Canadian industry.
In this particular round of tariff negotiations the provincial position is going to be relevant, because this time it will not simply be a matter of changing the Canadian tariff. Some provincial policies themselves will be the subject matter of criticism. Non-tariff barriers of various kinds to trade are up for negotiation at this time.
Since I have been Minister of Finance, I have noted one of the areas of difficulty has been not so much the policies of the federal government as the policies of various provincial governments which have been active in excluding foreign imports from Canada. I think, of course, of the policies of some liquor control boards, policies of other provincial entities with regard to government procurement, the policies of marketing boards, and so on. I think that kind of national discussion would be extremely valuable, not only for the purposes of obtaining

some indication of provincial priorities, but also for the purpose of learning what they are prepared to give up in terms of provincial protection in order to secure better markets for Canadian goods abroad.
Consultation with the private sector has been actively under way for over two years in the Canadian Tariffs and Trade Committee. That process of consultation will continue in the next six months as the Tokyo round of negotiations again gains momentum.
The hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Whittaker) spoke of the difficulties some Canadian manufacturers are experiencing in competing in the Canadian market, and said that one or more of them-this point was echoed by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen)-had moved their operation to the United States and were selling back to the Canadian market. That, really, is the crux of one of the major economic problems we face in Canada. Unless we can keep our costs down in this country, unless we can remain competitive on the world market, not just in the business of recreational homes to which the two hon. members referred, but in many other Canadian secondary manufacturing enterprises, our businessmen will want the future expansion of their businesses to take place outside this country. For that reason the government has put particular stress on the importance of restraining the increase of costs in this country and, particularly, restraining the increase in the rate of inflation.
The hon. member for Okanagan Boundary also referred to fresh fruits and vegetables, and referred positively to the report on fresh fruit and vegetables made by the Tariff Board and tabled recently by myself. The second part of that report on processed vegetables will be available in the early summer, and the two parts of that report will have an important role to play in forming the Canadian position with respect to negotiations at the Tokyo round, particularly negotiations with the United States.
Both the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary and the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) demonstrated the problems that the negotiators face, in the sense that at one time they were talking about better protection for Canadians and the next moment about better access to the American market. This is the basic problem that this country, indeed any country, faces in tariff negotiations.
What are you prepared to give up in the way of protection in Canadian industry for the purpose of getting better access to foreign markets? What are you prepared to trade off? That is the really critical question.
The hon. member for Wetaskiwin referred to the better market access he would seek for Alberta petrochemicals. That is a laudable objective if it can be achieved. He also talked about the importance of protecting certain Canadian agricultural markets in this country from penetration, particularly by United States exports. In this sense you have the contradiction that is involved in these negotiations for any country, of wanting better access for those products in which you think
May 17, 1977

you have a comparative advantage as opposed to having to give up protection of a certain Canadian industry.
On the question of vegetable oils, and indeed the question of further processing on the Great Plains, I would make a reference to the discussion which occurred in the question period with respect to the freight rate system and the impact of this on manufacturing in western Canada. It is a fair comment to make that indeed the crushers of rapeseed are faced with a difficult market in western Canada.
The problem is compounded by the fact that the freight rate system favours the shipment of either rapeseed, in the case of rapeseed crushers, or barley or other feed grains out of the Great Plains to be used not only in eastern Canada, but indeed for rapesseed to be processed in the Japanese market rather than having the processing occur in western Canada. There again is another trade-off you have to face between a lower freight rate for the raw product as opposed to the freight rate you have to pay for the more refined goods.
On the ad valorem beef tariff in the United States, the imbalance between the United States and the Canadian tariff, 1 recognize the imbalance. That is the kind of objective we should have in mind in going to the American negotiators, pointing out in this particular case we would be seeking reciprocal treatment in this regard, which I understand is the position the hon. member took. That is a very fair position. That is the kind of proposal we would have in a specific negotiation with the United States.
Finally, with regard to the machinery being imported by a small business, the present structure of the tariff system does make provision for the kind of situation to which the hon. member refers. There is a special provision with respect to machinery imports. If indeed it can be established that the piece of machinery being imported into Canada is not of a class or kind made in Canada and is not available from Canadian producers, that particular firm is able, under the machinery program, to make an application to get a remission of the duty. The hon. member did not mention any particular time frame within which the import had been made. If he would like to pursue with me a particular case of particular import, it may well be that under the machinery program they would be entitled to have back the duty which they have paid.
The hon. member for Surrey-White Rock made reference to the problem which he raised during the customs tariff bill debate last year, that is, with regard to the import of the elements by people who, as a matter of hobby, fill their own ammunition. As a result of the kind of representation he and others have made about importing things for hobbies in Canada, we have decided to make a reference to the Tariff Board to get their recommendation as to the appropriate treatment of imports of that kind for hobbies, and their being competitive with some of the products produced in Canada. That particular question is going to be given full consideration by the Tariff Board.
That covers some of the major items raised by hon. members. As we go through from clause to clause and look at the schedules, I will be glad to elaborate further.
Customs Tariff
