Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Ethier in the chair.
On clause 1.

Mr. Chairman, I thank the minister for his limited reference to my remarks on the Tariff Board report. However, he failed to tell us what input parliament will have in dealing with this report. What discussion will opposition members be able to have? Will this be dealt with through cabinet? Does it have to go to the GATT round in Geneva? There is quite a large area there on which I would certainly like an answer.

Yes, Mr. Chairman. What we have said in making the Tariff Board report public is that we would like to have reaction from the public. In particular, we would like reaction from those provincial governments such as Ontario and British Columbia which have made specific representation with regard to the tariff and other arrangements concerning fresh fruits and vegetables.
It would be very valuable within the context of this House to follow the practice that was followed about 1967 at the time the Kennedy round was under discussion and to have a discussion on the issues involved in the Kennedy round, in particular some of the trade-offs I was talking about, some of the things we have to pay in terms of tariff concessions in order to get concessions from others. Therefore, as the position becomes formulated with regard to the Canadian position abroad on the Kennedy round, I would be quite happy if we could find an appropriate order of reference to have this matter discussed in committee. Essentially, they are questions of detail, and discussion would be more appropriate there than in the House as a whole.
On the other hand, if the hon. member would like to make his views known, either personally or in writing, to me with regard to the fresh fruits and vegetables report, I would be delighted to have it in that form as well.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the minister about the function of the Tariff Board and the input that it might have in connection with the proposals in the bill before us. It became evident in committee that there is a great delay in the preparation of a report and the presentation or consideration of that report by the ministry. To begin with, perhaps the minister can tell us what the problem is with the delay that seems to be experienced, and also what kind of input there is from the Tariff Board itself to the ministry.

Mr. Chairman, I would have to concede that one of the first questions I raised when I became the minister was a question as to the relative lapse of time involved in some of these Tariff Board hearings. I think it can be said that a greater sense of urgency has been communicated to the new chairman of the board. Miss McDougall has set

May 17, 1977
Customs Tariff
some very much tighter time schedules for the production of the Board reports. A good example has been the production of the fresh fruits and vegetables report on which she has now delivered the first part, and we will be expecting the second part in the early summer. I have to correct myself, Mr. Chairman. We are not anticipating it, now, until the early fall. That is a good example, however, of the manner in which the Board's recommendation will become a basis for a policy decision by the department.
The Board has made recommendations with regard to fresh fruits and vegetables and described the way in which the tariff system is operating. We have sought public response to the Board's observations. Based on both the Board's observations and the public response, we shall go on to formulate the position to be taken in the Kennedy Round.
I give another example. The report of the Board on leisure craft has been available to the government for some time and specific items related to it are already in the government's portfolio for negotiation in the Tokyo Round. I have to say that to a great extent we have obviously been holding off in terms of making changes since many of our objectives in the negotiating round are objectives with regard to which we would prefer to withhold action until we find out the kind of return we can get. In other words, we do not want to give anything away at this point if by conceding it in the course of negotiations we can get better access for Canadian goods abroad.

Mr. Chairman, 1 have a news clipping from one of the Ottawa papers quoting the minister as saying that the next round of tariff negotiations will be "all too real". The gist of the article is that we are likely to find ourselves having to give a good deal away.
Bearing in mind the fact that many industries and producers in Canada believe that this country is a saint in a world of sinners as far as tariffs and trade are concerned, I should like to ask the minister this: do we intend to take a hard stand so that we are not the first to give things away as in the past? Will we be conceding tariff levels which are of importance to the electronics industry, for example, or mobile home manufacturers, or producers of farm products, to improve the position, say, of natural resources or CANDU reactors? Or will the minister go in with a hard line, such as I understand the United States intends to adopt, so that we may be able to put our unemployed to work in the manufacturing industry or in small business?

Mr. Chairman, I really should not be commenting in detail on the United States position, but I would have to say, on the basis of discussions with President Carter at the London summit meeting, that he was not going into the Tokyo Round with a hard line.
What about the U.S. Senate?

Well, the President has the authority under the existing legislation, and he does not intend to seek greater protectionism. 1 believe this is evident from his action with regard to the request made to him by the American shoe industry. An important reality, and one which we have to bear in mind, is this: at that London summit meeting, for example, we were the only country with access to a market of less than 100 million. The Americans, with a market of 220 million, are obviously in a position of much more "heft" when it comes to what they can press for and hope to get.
Having said that, I must add that on the basis of our experience in the last Kennedy Round we can expect to get better access to foreign markets. Our negotiators have proved to be very skillful. For example, we have proposed in certain of the sectors in which we have a comparative advantage, for instance, base metals and forest products, that current high tariff levels on more highly processed products in these areas where there are quota restrictions should be lifted so as to allow better access for Canadian exports. Indeed, we are looking to get better access for Canadian manufactured goods as well. But let us not be under any illusions that we shall not, in the next decade, be operating in a very tough competitive world.
We can expect no easy free rides in the negotiations. Nor can we expect to prevent others from penetrating our markets. The fact of the matter is that even with the relatively high levels of tariff in Canada in some areas, certain products from abroad have been able to sail right in over the top of the tariff wall. One example is textiles. We could, of course, say to our people, "We are going to pay more for everything around here; we are going to put the tariff walls very much higher and exclude foreign goods." The result would be restricted access for Canadian exports and a lower standard of living for everyone. It is a tough choice.
I understand the concern expressed by the hon. member but I do not think we can turn the clock back and go for higher tariff protection. In the first place, I am not sure Canadians are prepared to pay for it, and in the second place I am quite certain other countries will not permit us to get away with that kind of claim while expecting concessions from them in the negotiations.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Chairman, I thank the minister for his earlier answers. I would like to ask him about the Tariff Board again. I have a question concerning report No. 152 of the committee. It was conceded that the report was signed by the Tariff Board on March 2, 1977, although no attention appears to have been paid to it in the budget. It then came out that it was not until April 26 or thereabouts that the report was received from the printer and therefore the minister could not have had it in his possession until after the budget was presented on March 31.1 would like to ask the hon. gentleman what is the purpose of these reports which the minister receives from the Board, and when might some use be expected to be made of some of them.
May 17, 1977

I have answered that question by pointing out that the principal use of these reports will be in formulating the Canadian position in the Tokyo Round of negotiations. It would obviously be foolish to take up such a report, particularly if we are going to concede some points, before we get into the actual negotiation. For instance, in the case of the luxury craft we now have a good indication as to the structure of the industry and the kind of tariff treatment the Board thinks desirable. This is a report which we have in our portfolio for negotiation. That is why we have invited the views of the industry in Canada with regard to the Tariff Board's recommendations, and on the basis of this advice we shall formulate the Canadian position at the Tokyo Round.

Perhaps I could refer to report No. 149 on the pleasure craft, commissioned, I believe, in 1971. It took a long time to prepare. I cannot see the date. Anyway, it was received by the minister in April, 1976, some 11 months before his March 31 budget. That document was five years in production and it was in the hands of the department 11 months before the budget brought down in March of this year. According to the Chairman of the Tariff Board the minister has not included any of the pleasure craft recommendations in the current budget.
That is right, Mr. Chairman. As I said, that is again a matter for negotiation in the Tokyo round.

I know the minister gets a lot of representations from different groups with special interests, and in the debate on a similar bill last year I raised the matter of other interests which had been brought to the attention of the minister by myself and others. In this case it was the collection of vintage cars. I know there have been many representations made to the minister on this matter. It is argued that vintage cars are really no different from original works of art which are allowed into the country free of tariff, as are other things like antiques of a certain age. The minister has not seen fit to relieve vintage car hobbyists in Canada, even though they are trying to preserve in Canada some of Canada's history.
It has been a tradition in tariff setting in Canada that when there was a goods not of like kind produced in Canada, tariffs would not be prohibitive. It is a fact that many vintage car parts, particularly tires, are of a class or kind not made in Canada; at least they are not available in Canada. I would ask the minister what further consideration is going to be given this group of Canadians.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member said that we have done nothing about this. I would bring to his attention tariff item 69315-1 in which we have reduced the age of antiques, not just vintage cars, of all kinds, from 100 years to 50 years. As I indicated in my budget speech, we have also referred the various representations, which the hon. member has mentioned, in connection with antiques to the Tariff Board for their recommendation.
Customs Tariff

I was not aware, Mr. Chairman, that there were any automobiles approaching 100 years of age and I confess that bringing the limit down to 50 will certainly be a step in the right direction. Has the minister any thought of reducing it to something more realistic, such as 30 years of age for cars?
That is the kind of question which the Tariff Board will be considering.

Mr. Chairman, the questions that I should like to direct to the minister are primarily in the field of agriculture. He may feel that I am directing them to the wrong minister, but in view of the fact that in an earlier debate on the same subject not too many years ago I asked the Minister of Agriculture whether he had been consulted about changes in duties and reduction of protection for agricultural products and he said no, and I asked the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs whether he had estimated or in any way calculated the benefits to Canada, or the disadvantages to Canada, resulting from reduction in tariffs on agricultural items and had it been part of his input into the duty structure as it related to change in that budget, and he said no, I therefore assumed that the government must have made some calculation as to the impact upon the total Canadian economy of a reduction of protection for Canadian products.
I should like to ask the minister whether reductions in duty on agricultural items have been related to their effectiveness on imports into Canada, and has there been any tabulation of the comparable effect of duty in markets to which we might ship, or the comparable effect of duty in places where similar items are produced and imports are regulated by protection? Has there been any calculation to determine whether or not Canada is being fair to itself in this change in duty structure?

Mr. Chairman, I find the question a little obscure in the sense of asking have we calculated the impact in other markets to which we ship. I would have to say with regard to our own tariff that probably the best evidence of the fact that Canadian producers have not suffered unduly is that, on the whole, there have not been extensive representations against these particular temporary tariff reductions which, as I have said, have now been in place for close to four years. There have been a number of cases where there were representations in the past and we had taken action for the purpose of restoring the duty. A good example of that is the action that we took earlier this year with regard to pork.
In general terms it is difficult to make a precise calculation of the kind of saving to the consumer resulting from the reduction of the tariff. On the other hand, one can say at the same time very clearly that if the customer does not have passed on to him the additional cost of a number of points of duty, then it is going to cost him less.

So in other words, Mr. Chairman, the answer is no, there has been no study of the relative effect of duty on agricultural products brought into Canada versus the effect of duty levied on agricultural products which might go to other

May 17, 1977
Customs Tariff
markets, such as the European Economic community or to the United States, which is a recipient of some of our exports. 1 guess the answer is no, there has been no study to determine the effectiveness of our duty versus the effectiveness of duties in other jurisdictions, and this is what I had suspected from the beginning.
I should like to ask the minister why he feels there should be restrictions on the importation of textiles, for instance, which will have exactly the impact, so far as food is concerned, which the minister has denounced. A relative impact on clothing will be felt, as there would be a relative impact on food if agricultural products had had greater protection. Why does the minister feel that textiles and some other items in Canada deserve increased protection, either by an increment in the effective duty or by the restriction of imports by quota, as is the case in the textile industry? Why should these industries be isolated and agriculture left out?

Mr. Chairman, the principal reason is that there had been a dramatic increase in textile imports into Canada, to the point where imported textiles had come to assume about 55 per cent of the Canadian market. We are talking of an industry that employs 200,000 people. We recognize that there will have to be a substantial adjustment for both firms and work force in adjusting to the current terms of trade whereby particularly more advanced developing countries can now sell effectively into our market even over the existing tariff structure. However, the feeling was that the situation had reached crisis point in that particular industry and that we should give them temporary protection until the adjustments can be made.
The Canadian textile industry has already been through one adjustment when it reduced non-competitive capacity in the 1960's and early 1970's. It is now faced with very much the same thing again. It is important for the employees involved, on a temporary basis, to protect their present jobs as far as possible, and then make the effort to give them adjustment assistance to move into other areas of the economy, a task upon which the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce is now engaged.

I think the minister is improving the case for agriculture as he goes along. There is a distinct parallel between the textile industry and certain facts of the agricultural industry. I would ask him to take a sincere and deep look as Minister of Finance at some of the alarming alterations in trade patterns as a result of some of our negotiations in the international world of trade. Take, for instance, the apple industry. Does the minister have any idea of the change in the pattern of the apple trade over the last 25 years, part of which results from international negotiations or the establishment of unnatural barriers in markets to which we had at one time exported substantial quantities of apples and which are now closed to us?

Mr. Chairman, indeed that is recognized. One of the substantial markets was certainly that of the United Kingdom. We have lost our advantage with regard to many agricultural products in that market because of the United Kingdom's accession to the European Economic Community. That is not a matter of negotiation we could have prevented by withholding in some way. The United Kingdom was in a position to make its own decision to join the EEC. It was entitled to do so under GATT, and it did do so. That is a kind of change in international events for which one cannot provide protection. One has to seek to provide adjustment assistance. It is fair to say in many of the agricultural programs a parallel type of adjustment assistance has been provided.

Mr. Chairman, I agree the items I will refer to have been the extreme reflectors of the pattern, but they have at the same time reflected upon important segments of the field of agriculture. Is the minister aware, for instance, that in the ten year period from 1966 to 1975 apple imports increased from 54 million pounds in 1966 to 148 million pounds, or almost threefold? Is the minister aware of the source of the pressure upon Canadian apple production?
I submit the aid which has been given to the textile industry is not drawn from the public treasury, nor does agriculture appreciate the fact that as a result of some of the positions in which it finds itself it must draw from the public treasury if it is to remain viable at all in certain products which are native to this country. In past years there were fair and equitable trade agreements, and we have been major exporters and able to supply all of our own requirements. The apple is the extreme case as a result of these things. When you go from 54 million pounds to 148 million pounds of imports in a ten year period, you find it very serious to accept. If you look at the export picture in that same commodity for a comparable period of time, you will find our exports declined by something like 31 million pounds. This puts us in a very unfavourable net position. If I were to take this back 25 years, the figures would be even more alarming.
Is it not reasonable for the Canadian apple producer to ask for treatment comparable to that of the cheese producer or the textile producer of Canada, so that he might have a chance to flourish within an area of his own country?
Mr. Chairman, the Tariff Board report we have been discussing this evening recommends apples should continue to come in duty free.

That has been the very generous position which has been adopted over the years by the apple industry; but it was also assuming, when it made this recommendation, that it would not lose equal trading opportunities in jurisdictions to which it had exported over the years, and these have been lost. Therefore there is demand upon the public treasury for support in the apple industry.

May 17, 1977

Let us go to a crop which is not as major in significance. Is the minister aware that in the same ten year period there has been almost a threefold increase in the import of cherries as far as Canada is concerned?
Mr. Chairman, I would have to check to see if the hon. member's figures are correct.
Is the minister aware that the increase in importing pears has been in the region of 45 per cent in the same ten year period?
Mr. Chairman, with regard to cherries and with regard to pears, the Tariff Board has made precise recommendations, on which the hon. gentleman might like to comment.
You have them in front of you.
You have the Tariff Board report.

When you look at onions, in that same ten year period the importation changed from 63 million to 96 million which was an increase of over 50 per cent and a physical increase of 33 million in round figures. Mr. Chairman, I should point out I am referring to pounds throughout.
Is the minister aware that in the tomato industry imports have gone up 48 million pounds in the same ten year period? Is the minister aware that, as a result of the position considered as a crop which Canadian farmers should drop because the effective tariff structure is such that it can neither be grown nor processed effectively in Canada at this point in time and may be wiped from the scene?

Mr. Chairman these are commodities which have been dealt with by the Tariff Board report. One of the purposes of having that report is to get a judicial balance, and we have got it. This is one of the questions now being discussed with the agricultural industry. A most helpful thing at this particular point would be, if the hon. gentleman disagrees with the Tariff Board report in this regard, for him to indicate the ways in which we could do so. If he feels these particular interests need help, then I think the most useful thing he can do is to express the kind of help needed and comment on the statement which has been made respecting fresh fruit and vegetables.

Mr. Chairman, I should point out for the minister's information that I have been a regular attendant at the Canadian Horticultural Council for approximately 30 years. I am familiar with the demands they have made and the treatment they have received. Notwithstanding what the tariff report may say, I would like to draw another crop to the minister's attention. Before doing so, 1 should say the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, the Minister of Agriculture, and the government itself should not seek the crutches of various boards as the government tries to justify its position in an intolerable situation created by trade policies which are not related to the needs of Canadian
Customs Tariff
industry in any way, shape or form. Certain aspects have absolutely been demoralized in our trade structure and our agricultural production. If you take a look at the figure for tomatoes 25 years back compared to today, they would starkly point out to the minister that fresh and processed tomatoes, both in relation to our capacity to produce and in relation to our nation consuming that product, are an industry which is no longer significant as an agricultural crop. We are relying on foreign sources to produce what we can produce in our own gardens at home. This is not good government policy, whether you want to use the Tariff Boards as a crutch or an excuse for the things which have been visited upon agriculture. The minister has not studied the matter, as he revealed in his first answer to me.
In the ten year period imports of broccoli went up from nine million pounds to 34 million pounds. That is an increase of more than 350 per cent in the importation of broccoli in a ten year period. If one were to take a look at strawberries, as I mentioned earlier, that item has disappeared as a Canadian agricultural product relative to Canadian consumption. I believe these figures are somewhat rounded. I did not bring one piece of paper which I should have brought with me. The importation of fresh and frozen strawberries has risen from five million pounds in 1952 to approximately 55 million in 1976. That is an elevenfold increase in imports of one product.
I support the minister as he protects the textile industry. 1 supported him when he took belated action with respect to pork. It was belated, but it was a step in the right direction. But 1 cannot support a policy under which producers in Canada should suffer because of a lack of protection, where we find the doors closed in traditional markets and we open our doors to rather non-traditional sources of meat. These things have been said in the Standing Committee on Agriculture as strongly as possible. If the minister would read the resolutions and recommendations as they have been presented by the Horticultural Council over the last 30 years, he would find that that council predicted exactly what has happened.
I would like to ask one other question of the minister. How many agricultural jobs have been lost and how many jobs in the processing industry have been lost as a result of these changes which have taken place, and in relation to the percentage of crops we now produce along with the percentage of crop which we ourselves can consume and which other countries can consume? How many jobs have been lost in Canada? We protected the textile industry. We should have protected agriculture on a broader base. Has the minister made any study whatsoever as to the impact on employment of reduced agricultural products in the broad scope of things agricultural over the last 25 years when we have had a cheap food policy and an open door policy for trade?

Mr. Chairman, there is no doubt about the fact that there has been a substantial drop in employment in agriculture, just as there has been a substantial

May 17, 1977
Customs Tariff
drop in employment in the textile industry. The hon. gentleman says we have protected the textile industry.
As you should have.

He forgets the fact that by a series of steps taken in the late sixties and early seventies we made a very substantial restructuring of that industry as a result of which a significant number of plants were closed and people were moved into other areas of employment in the economy. It seems to me that was the sensible way to manage things, and that is the way it was managed at the time.
Going back to the hon. member's comment when he said we should not have a Tariff Board-
I did not say you should not have; I said you should not use it as a crutch.

Accepting the recommendations of the Tariff Board, considering them, asking for public consultation on them, and on the basis of all that deciding on our negotiating position-is that using the Board as a crutch? It seems to me that if the Board has, as it has, devoted many hours to taking testimony from many interests in this regard, it is entitled to be listened to by the government. The Board is listened to by the government. It makes sense to have the Board part of the process, and this has been recognized by governments for many years.

Mr. Chairman, I agree basically with what the minister said, but he did not go far enough. As far as he went he was correct. It is the function of the Tariff Board to make recommendations to the government, but it is the responsibility of the government to make decisions after having faced the economic realities of this nation as a whole.
The minister has expressed concern in various dissertations which he has given both inside the House and outside with respect to the impact of an unfavourable balance of trade. Has the minister taken a serious look at what an element of protection for agriculture could do to change the imbalance of trade which we are presently experiencing? With the exception of grains for the moment, because we must agree that grains are at an unusual peak in value, has the minister taken a look at the balance of trade as it relates to food, and particularly food which we can produce in this country, and its impact upon the total economy of the nation? Has there been any precise study in that field?

Mr. Chairman, very obviously the Tariff Board has focused on that, and that is quite a precise study. I think it is fair to observe that for very many months of the year in Canada the Canadian producer is not in a position to supply the Canadian market with fresh fruits and vegetables. Very obviously these are the commodities which, given almost any circumstances, we will be importing into this country.
I did not mention bananas, lemons or grapefruit. 1 mentioned crops.

I just have one more question, Mr. Chairman.

speechtext: The hon. member will be allowed one more question.

You have been very generous, Mr. Chairman, and I appreciate it.
Does the minister know that the importation of agricultural products from 1960-64, on a five year average, to 1975, went from roughly $780 million to roughly $2.8 billion, a $2 billion increase in imports of food into this country?

Mr. Chairman, I do know that there has been a substantial improvement in our standard of living generally, and the hon. member will find a similar escalation in that regard through the same period. I suppose the question is whether Canadians should be entitled to import lettuce or fresh tomatoes in the winter time, and we think they are.
Take a look at these things.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to comment briefly on the apple situation which is a good example of what happens when we negotiate with other countries such as the United States to take tariffs off over a period of years. It was agreed to take it off over a period of years, but the then minister of finance decided that he was going to take it off completely in Canada, so within one year he took the tariff off. He asked the United States to take theirs off as well, but because of the agreement they refused to do so. So there we were in Canada trading with no tariff on the commodity coming into Canada, and we had to pay one. However, over those years there was a constant increase of imports of apples into Canada, and as the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte said, starting out on an equal basis of probably one million boxes going out of Canada and one million boxes coming in, now, ten years later, it costs us three times as much. We have free trade in apples. The farmer in his orchard is not protected, but many industries on which he depends are protected.
For instance, the Minister of Agriculture put a complete barrier in front of farmers going down into the United States to bring back sprays. Farmers are trying to compete when the industries on which they depend are working in a climate of protection, and it is getting more and more difficult. I am quite aware that the industry did not ask for a tariff and that therefore the Tariff Board did not say that there should be a tariff put on our apples; however, I am also aware of the stabilization that is needed today in the apple industry because of this situation. I am also aware that it is difficult to market this commodity because of imports coming into Canada. Three times the previous amount of this commodity is now being imported into Canada.
May 17, 1977

I would like to comment on the cherry situation. The minister asked the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte if he would like to comment on it. I am very aware of what is in the Tariff Board report with regard to cherries. On Sunday I was down in the fruit markets of Ottawa. 1 saw a sign in a window which said "Cherries, 89 cents". 1 thought that we really are going to get cheap cherries this year. I took a closer look and found that the price was 89 cents per half pound. Cherries from the United States are selling in Ottawa at SI.68 to $1.79 per pound. We would sure like to get that kind of market for our Canadian cherries. Those prices will not change very much until just about the time Canadian cherries come on the market. By that time 85 per cent of the cherry production of the United States will have been sold. The remaining 15 per cent is then sold at a much lower price. It is the tail end that they are getting rid of, and it is with that that the Canadian producer has to compete. It is a very short market season for cherries. We grow a good product and we are using the type of farm land that people are saying today should be frozen, should not be paved over or have houses built on it.
In this tariff report there is also a report on the surcharge concept that the farmers producing commodities such as cherries and peaches need and are requesting. One of the disappointing features of the report is that the Tariff Board only recommended that it be triggered at 85 per cent of the three-year average. It is doubtful that on a monthly basis 85 per cent of the three-year average will be enough to give the necessary protection for that short period when United States producers will ship into Canada at a lesser price than they are getting today.
We will be into the Canadian peach season within 40 or 50 days and growers are going to need help of this kind this year. If the report is going to gather dust for a while it is not going to be of any use to producers this year. I should like to request that the minister look at the surcharge provisions that have been used before by the government and that are recommended for use now, and put them into effect for this year's crop.

Mr. Chairman, in a previous customs tariff debate 1 made reference to western crops of flax and the 50 cents per bushel duty on flax going into the United States while there is no duty on flax coming into Canada. Flax is a cash crop for western Canadian producers and it is a useful crop. Last fall about 2 million bushels were exported to the United States. 1 am not sure why, because the price tends to be the same in both countries. It is a small volume crop compared to wheat, and this sort of thing happens. The flax growing area of the United States is the Dakotas so perhaps that is why it moved back and forth across the border. There is no particular reason, however, why the United States should impose a 50 cents per bushel duty when we do not impose any. It would be desirable to have the United States remove the duty so that there could be a free flow back and forth. If this cannot be done it would seem logical that we should have the same duty.
Customs Tariff
Reports from the negotiations in Tokyo seem quite pessimistic and little progress seems to have been made. It is disconcerting that according to a report in the Globe and Mail, little progress has been made in agriculture which includes such sub-groups as dairy, meat, grain and other products. Some agricultural producers feel that they have been used as a trade-off and that their interests have been subordinated to manufacturing or resource industries. Does the minister feel this is happening at Tokyo now, or has there been a change in emphasis?

Mr. Speaker, in general terms I would have to say that the Tokyo Round discussions on agriculture have not made very much progress up to this point. This is principally because of the stalemate between the United States and the EEC on agricultural products and the manner in which they would be negotiated in the Tokyo Round. There was some indication at the London summit meetings that this impasse might now be broken and there was some prospect of having early negotiations in substance in the Tokyo Round. It is quite true there has been less progress on agriculture, than, for example, on manufactured products or the preparatory work done concerning some of the other questions which will be negotiated in this round.
On the matter of flax, I think the hon. member makes a good case, just as a good case was made by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin with regard to boxed beef as to an imbalance between the Canadian and United States tariffs. If one looks at that particular sector there could be powerful argument with the Americans about reciprocity. The difficulty with picking one element out of a complicated structure like tariffs is that you cannot be sure where else in the schedule of tariffs they may seek reciprocity which may have a very substantial impact on Canadian producers.
This is the kind of trade-off that will occur. I cannot say whether flax or boxed beef is on the list for negotiation, but very obviously the MTN, the Tokyo Round, is the basis for trying to get reciprocity on these items.
In our negotiations in Tokyo, on the agricultural products do we tend to be on the side of the Americans in dealing with the EEC, or do we have our own stance?

Mr. Chairman, it depends on what the product is. If it is one in which we are seeking substantial access to the American market, obviously we will be looking at it on a bilateral basis. Equally obviously, if there is a product that the Americans are interested in and where they can use their much greater weight because of the size of their market to penetrate the EEC, it makes sense for us to let the American lineman run interference for the Canadian back fielder. On the MFN quality, the generalization for other contracting parties of a negotiated rate or quota arrangement between the United States and the EEC, we can get the benefit of the lower rate without having to pay anything for it. It really depends on the commodity and what the prospects are for selling it. Obviously we are going to have important bilateral trade with the Americans, and equally we are going

to be looking forward to the possibility of their making some penetration of the European market, of which we will get the benefit through the MFN clause. There will be some third commodities for which, obviously we will have to carry the ball ourselves.

On the question of countervailing duties there is a suggestion that Canada continue to press for injury to domestic industry as a key criterion, contrary to the practice of the United States. I should like to ask the minister what the difference is in our approach to these countervailing duties and how is this working out?

Mr. Chairman, 1 am reminded that fresh regulations have just been issued with regard to countervailing duties. The hon. gentleman is correct in saying that the Canadian practice required the identification of injury, whereas the American practice had been mandatory. The new regulations we have put forward make provision for interim duties, pending the ultimate finding of injury. In other words, in a practical sense we are moving closer to the American position, but there is still this difference between the two positions.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask one more question concerning the United States treasury and the court case involving Zenith Radio Corporation? According to what I read in newspapers, the consequences of that case, which is still before the courts, could be serious. Do the minister and his officials regard that as a serious case, with wide-ranging tariff and trade implications?
Mr. Chairman, I would have to say yes, but cannot give a detailed explanation why.

Mr. Chairman, 1 hope I am not out of order; I was attending a committee meeting when the Minister of Finance made his summary comments winding up the second reading debate. I wonder if he dealt with the question of the component parts of shells used for target practice. What are his plans in this regard and, if he does not plan to allow this item in tariff free, will he explain his reasons for his decision?

Mr. Chairman, I dealt with the question and indicated that this is one item with respect to which we have sought the advice of the Board. We want to know how to treat hobby items of this kind. The question is now under consideration by the Tariff Board which is looking at how the matter is to be treated.
Mr. Chairman, can the minister indicate when he will have an answer or decision from the Tariff Board and announce it in the House?
Mr. Chairman, I cannot give an indication of an early response. The Board will be considering the question, but I am afraid I do not know what the timetable is.

Mr. Speaker, may I address a question to the minister? I hope my question will be in order. It concerns the importation from the United States of fabrics which, if made in Canada, would naturally be subject to tariff. I am talking about a double knit fabric which is normally made in Canada. If there is a backing on it, it is used for upholstery purposes. I understand such a material with backing is not made in Canada, and that a tariff is imposed on such imported double knit fabric which, with a special backing, is used only for upholstery. Have I correctly described the effect of our present regulations?

Mr. Chairman, I am afraid I cannot give a specific answer this evening with regard to the application of that tariff item. Certainly I could inquire and enlighten the hon. gentleman. Collectively, the trio in the committee of which I am a member cannot respond to that specific question.

Mr. Chairman, I return to the Tokyo Round, which the minister discussed a few moments ago and about which the hon. member for Dauphin questioned him. I, and 1 am sure my comments apply to others, have received letters from manufacturers in my constituency and the surrounding area concerning the Tokyo Round. The tenor of such letters makes it clear that manufacturers do not know what is happening. They have made submissions to the minister but there has been no feedback. They are operating in the dark, not knowing if they can expand operations and put in another production line, or if the negotiations will lead to a drop in tariffs, with possibly unfortunate consequences for certain products. I understand that Mr. Gray is shortly to return from Geneva. What is the government doing to let industry- know what is happening in tariffs? Is the minister planning to hold meetings, or to hold further discussions, or to issue press releases concerning the progress of negotiations? We need to know what is happening in this area.

Mr. Chairman, the Canadian Trade and Tariffs Committee was specifically set up for this purpose. It has received submissions from Canadian industry and, indeed, has met with representatives of Canadian firms who have sought such meetings, as, indeed, Rod Gray has on his fairly frequent return visits to Canada. The hon. member suggested that there is an element of uncertainty with regard to certain products as a result of negotiations. I think, inevitably, there will be a certain amount of uncertainty until the negotiations are finalized. For reasons of which I am sure the hon. gentleman is aware, the discussions have stood still for a time. There is now some prospect, after the meeting of two weeks-ago, that they will be moving forward somewhat more quickly. However, until the final deal is made there will be that element of uncertainty. The Tariffs and Trade Committee intends to try to resolve such difficulties as best it can in addition to being an effective communications medium.

Mr. Chairman, may I refer the minister to the report by the Tariff Board, known as Reference No. 150, which deals with computers and related telecommunications
May 17, 1977

equipment? Let me give the minister some background. I hope the minister can bring the committee up to date on the government's current position with respect to the tariff structure affecting computers and related telecommunications equipment.
It is interesting to note that Hon. E. J. Benson on December 10, 1971, requested the Tariff Board to prepare this report, which was finally signed on March 3, 1977, by a board the composition of which was somewhat different from that to which Mr. Benson had originally addressed his request some five years and three months earlier. I raise this matter because some in the computer field have told me that their industry has changed. Some of the people previously active in it and who were witnesses have died, retired or resigned. The Board's delay in reporting is most strange. A minister of finance requested this report several years ago; now, two ministers of finance later, so to speak, the Board has finally handed down its report.
This report says substantially this "Guess what? What you said back in 1971 concerning the computer industry was quite right." My question is this: since we will have waited five years and five months by the time the report will be tabled in the House, let me now ask the minister what does the government intend to do to relieve the computer industry from the senseless customs duty which, as the Tariff Board seems to agree, that industry has been forced to pay over the years?
Let me refer to the letter Mr. Benson sent on December 10, 1971, to the then chairman of the Tariff Board, Mr. L. C. Audette, Q.C. He said that he received representations concerning the effect of the customs tariff on the production and use of computers and related equipment, and went on to say:
It has also been alleged that the duty on such equipment, especially that which is not available in Canada, is having an adverse effect on the ability of the Canadian business community to take advantage of computer services and techniques and discourages the processing of data in Canada.
Five years and some months later, the Tariff Board handed down its report. At page 325 of its report the Board begins to make that part of its recommendation which says that the tariff on the items alluded to should be changed or reduced. The Board stated on page 325 of the report:
Given the pattern that characterizes the Canadian computing equipment industry, the Board has carefully weighed the available evidence and concludes that the tariff has had very little effect in restricting imports, supporting a viable Canadian-owned indusry, or in influencing production location decisions ...
The report goes on to say:
The Board has found no evidence to support the need for a general level of tariff protection on all finished computer products.
When we questioned the Chairman of the Tariff Board as to what recommendations made in the past the Minister of Finance has implemented, we were left with the strong impression that there has been little interplay between the activities of the Minister of Finance and those of the Tariff Board. In short, although it takes years to prepare these reports, they are conveniently filed away and little reference is made to them. This is most unfortunate.
Customs Tariff
If we look, we find that 34 different people or companies actually made submissions to the Tariff Board as to why the tariffs on computer and related equipment should be changed. It is most unfortunate that the Minister of Finance seems to be so casual toward Tariff Board reports after they have been prepared.
I notice tonight the minister stated that the government is entitled, and I think I have his words correctly, to listen when the Tariff Board speaks. That is the point, Mr. Chairman. I understand that technically the minister can amend what we have before us tonight and can give effect to the Tariff Board recommendations here tonight as far as the computer industry is concerned. My first question is, is he willing to do that, bearing in mind it took the Tariff Board five years and three months to sign a report that was transmitted to him a month later?

Mr. Chairman, I think one of the important points to make in this regard and one of the reasons for tabling it in parliament is so that industry will have an opportunity to comment. As the hon. member knows, the document was tabled several weeks ago. We will be looking forward to comment.
Will 1 be prepared to take the tariffs off this evening? For the very reasons I indicated before the hon. member came into the House, I would have some hesitation in doing that. We are going into an international negotiation in which we will have to give up some things in order to get other things. If we are going to reduce the Canadian tariff for somebody else's benefit, we should try to get something for it.
Far from being casual about it, we have, for example with regard to pleasure craft and other representations, kept any possible changes as one of the matters on which we would be prepared to negotiate in the multilateral trade negotiations rather than giving them away unilaterally before the negotiations are completed.

Following on the minister's reply, will he now indicate what steps he will actually take? We now have in hand a Tariff Board report which recommends a reduction in tariffs on computers. What is the next step? It was tabled not a few weeks ago as the minister indicated, but within the last ten days. What happens now? Is there any formal exchange between here and Geneva where the report is drawn to the attention of those people, with or without a recommendation of the minister?
Second, what process is the minister going to follow to ensure that those who are affected by the report and know of it have an opportunity to make their feelings known? I ask this because I have checked with some of these companies. To date, most of them do not even know that the report has been tabled in the House.

Mr. Chairman, I have to say that the Tariff Board gave publicity to the fact that it produced the report. If companies which took the trouble to make

Customs Tariff
submissions in this regard have not been following the issue that closely, then I suppose I should ask the Tariff Board to go back to those who made a submission and bring this to their attention. The Board has, however, publicized the fact that it has reported. As I indicated, we are seeking public response to it at this time. Obviously the government will have to make a judgment on what to do in this regard, in particular on how to treat it in the MTN negotiations.
The next step, in answer to the specific question, is to get the public response to the Board's findings and evaluate this response to see to what extent the government should either, in its conclusion, change those findings, or be prepared to accept as the Board has recommended.

Following on the minister's comments, Mr. Chairman, will he indicate specifically how he is going to seek the public response? Is it going to be to all individual companies that are listed here, something over 100 of them? Is the onus on them to come to the minister? Is so, how long does he plan to wait until he feels they have had a fair opportunity to respond before we can hear what his views are on the Tariff Board's recommendation?

Mr. Chairman, I think it is not unreasonable, having given it some publicity, that we should be able to assume that within this industry there will be some knowledge of the report and that the people who want to respond will be coming forward. Any interested person can come forward and make representations in this regard. Publicity is obviously the sensible way to bring this to their attention.
It is fair enough to give those interested a matter of weeks, perhaps a matter of several months, to formulate their response. We in turn are going to be hardening our own position on the negotiations as the year goes on. It would obviously be advisable if they responded as quickly as they could.

The minister refers to publicity having been given to the tabling of this report by the Tariff Board. 1 ask this advisedly. Will the minister now advise precisely what was the nature of the publicity the Tariff Board gave to the report?
Mr. Chairman, there was a press release and a notice of where copies of the report could be acquired.
Is the minister aware that the total number of copies available was 40, in spite of the fact that at one time almost 200 concerns were interested in what the Tariff Board might have to say?
Mr. Chairman, I think I will have to check on the accuracy of that. I would certainly be prepared to question it.
If I understand it correctly, the minister intends to wait a few months until, as he says, he hardens his attitude.
Position.
What exactly then is the process? I take it this may or may not be dealt with at Geneva, depending on how his process hardens. Is that correct?
Yes.

May I get to the more general question of what is being changed in Bill C-55. Will the minister give us an indication as to how he decides, notwithstanding the Geneva negotiations, to change certain items but not to change other items? For example, I notice that peanut butter in this bill is now going to be free of any tariff whatsoever.
In Bill C-15, which was given first reading October 22, 1976, peanut butter was subject to a tariff of two cents in so far as the British preferential tariff was concerned, two cents in so far as the most favoured nation was concerned, and seven cents on the general tariff. That is all per pound.
What caused the minister in the case of peanut butter to say we will change the tariff as of now, whereas in so far as the computer industry, the small boats industry and what not are concerned, this is something to be dealt with only in Geneva?

Mr. Chairman, I dealt with this earlier today. This was an item dealt with at Geneva. As I indicated in my statement earlier today, as part of the multilateral trade negotiations it was agreed that a range of products of specific interest to the developing countries would be dealt with on an early basis and would not be held up until the end of the negotiations under the MTN. This peanut butter item happens to be one of them, as indeed are quite a number of products, many of them related to products agricultural or other products of a tropical origin.
The minister clarified the situation with regard to peanut butter. Is the list available of what has been left open for tariff reductions with no particular reference to the Geneva negotiations?
Mr. Chairman, if I can just correct the hon. member, I said it was decided at the Geneva negotiations and the list is in the bill.

May I assume from the minister's response that the entire list is in the bill and the bill includes nothing that is not in the document he is referring to as being exempted by the Geneva negotiations?

Again I dealt with this on second reading, pointing out the different categories of items being dealt with in the bill. There are three. The hon. member might like to examine the record in this regard. This is the list of items agreed on at the multilateral trade negotiations between the contracting parties and has been included in the bill. There will be further negotiations. It may indeed be that further negotiations might provide a further list of items for the benefit of the developing countries. At the moment this is what has been agreed upon and is included in our law.

May 17, 1977

That is just the point. What has been agreed upon? The minister's official is nodding his head in the negative. The minister is saying that what is in the bill has been agreed upon. What I am trying to relate is not what the minister said on second reading, but what is in the bill now before us. What specifically has been included in the exemption that the minister referred to with regard to the Geneva negotiations? Is it the entire bill, every item in there or is it certain items and not other items?
When the last tariff bill was before us I directed the minister's attention to item No. 8717-1 dealing with onions. 1 pointed out that there seemed to be an unfair tariff arrangement between the United States and ourselves in that the duty on Canadian onions going into the United States was one and three-quarter cents per pound while the duty on onions coming into this country, as we can see in the bill before us tonight, was 1 Vi cents. As that time the minister stated he was unaware of the U.S. duty position. Can he now give us this information? Has he checked it out? If there is this relatively unfair duty arrangement as far as the two countries are concerned can he tell us why we have been going along with a relatively favourable duty position as far as onions are concerned?

Mr. Chairman, fresh fruits and vegetables are the subject of the Tariff Board reference. As 1 indicated in response to earlier questions it is a matter which is now open for comment by interested parties in Canada. It is obviously a question which will be included in the negotiations. Whether we shall be able to get reciprocity of treatment is something which will have to await the outcome of the negotiations.
I think it should be said, in general terms, that there is a longer period of the year in which it is to our advantage to import onions in comparison to the period of time in which we would be in a position to export from Canadian production. This is one of the factors to be taken into account in the temporary tariff reductions.
More specifically, though, could the minister tell us whether his research has disclosed that the American duty is in fact higher than ours on produce going into the United States?
Mr. Chairman, that answer will take just a moment. Yes.

Mr. Chairman, there is an interesting item on page 29, Schedule III, at the bottom of the page. It has to do with ivory carvings. I refer to the schedule which appears to apply to the developing countries. Would the minister explain what is happening in this connection? Is the tariff going down on this item?

The tariff is being reduced. Ivory carvings are included in a group of handicrafts which are among the exports of certain developing countries. When
Customs Tariff
imported into Canada they will be given the same treatment as other items under the MFN rate.

I find it very strange that at this time Canada should be reducing tariffs on ivory carvings. We all know that the United States has placed a ban on imports of ivory and bone carvings done by our Eskimos. It applies to all artifacts made from bone, even though in most instances they are made from fossil and are very old. It makes it difficult for our Eskimo people to trade or sell their products; their market is pretty well confined to Canada. This seems to me to be another example of people who practice a fine art finding other countries banning their products while at the same time Canada is reducing tariffs on similar items coming into Canada.

Perhaps I might remind the hon. member that this applies to just a specific group of countries, that is, the developing countries. It is part of a policy followed by Canada and other OECD nations under which we have agreed that in order to further the economic development of the developing world we should open our markets to their products. Ivory carvings reflect in a real way the cultural differences which exist in African countries and it does not follow we should in some way exclude them because a third party is excluding a product made by Canadian sculptors.
I must say I regret the exclusion of Canadian handicrafts and believe it to be a rather foolish practice. However, it does not seem to me we should take revenge on developing countries just because certain Canadian exports happen to be handled in this way. If this involved perfectly standard goods where there was no difference in utility, quality or style from one to the other, there might be some validity to the argument. But ivory carvings are obviously a reflection of a culture, and in that sense one who is interested in Eskimo carvings might not necessarily be interested in these ivory carvings. When you get right down to it, I suppose it is really a case of whether you wish to help the developing countries or not.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to introduce a discordant note, but perhaps the minister could give us the timetable he has in mind as to the changeover in the customs tariff to the metric system. We are already dealing with kilograms while at the same time referring to ounces and pounds. It is my understanding that in September we are to adopt the linear metre in Canada. I think that somewhere here I could undoubtedly find some reference to the inch, the foot, and the yard. Perhaps the minister could tell us when it is planned to convert into the metric system.
No specific date has yet been determined. I think we may be looking as far ahead as two years from now.

Mr. Chairman, I have had a chance to look at item 69315-1 concerning articles produced more than 50 years prior to a certain date. I should like to ask whether the word "articles" does, in fact, include automobiles, and whether the

May 17, 1977
Customs Tariff
word "goods" used on page 36 of Schedule IV, the first word in tariff item 70320-1, also includes automobiles?
The answer to both questions is yes.

May I also inquire whether any provision has been made in connection with parts and tires for these automobiles? I asked earlier about the "class or kind" wording and I note that the wording used on page 34 in reference to aircraft engines is "when of types or sizes not made in Canada". Further down on the same page, referring to parts for metric conversion, I see the wording "parts when of types or sizes not made in Canada". I am not sure what the difference between "class or kind" and "types or sizes" is. What about parts for these old cars which are now able to come in free?
Such parts if recently manufactured would not, of course, be antique and would have to be dealt with in the normal way under the tariff.
1 see that argument, but what about the idea of class or kind and types or sizes not made in Canada? Will that not apply to parts for these old automobiles?
It will depend on the type of tariff item they come in under. It may or may not have that kind of qualification.

Another item which has been brought to my attention is 70320-1, having to do with goods acquired by a former resident of Canada returning to Canada. I suppose my question hangs on the interpretation of the word "acquire" which appears in the phrase "was acquired after March 31, 1977". It may be strange, but I have two constituents who both find themselves in the position of taking a year's leave from Canada. Obviously this was planned for some months; you do not plan this kind of thing in no time at all. Both had gone on the basis of the existing tariff and had acquired boats or yachts, one from England and the other from Korea. In any event, these vessels were acquired, they think-at least, the money was paid and the contract signed-prior to March 31. They are now very concerned because they have not yet taken delivery but the acquisition has been made. Will these vessels be subject to duty on the excess value over $7,500, or will they be admitted under the old tariff?

I am being asked to give a judgment in a particular case. I think it would be wiser to have the full facts, and if the hon. member would write me a letter I would be prepared to get an opinion from National Revenue in this regard. In general terms, Mr. Chairman, acquisition assumes the taking of possession, but there may be facts which could support another interpretation.

1 thank the minister for that answer. On my advice these individuals have written to the department for an

answer, but I thought this was the opportune time to ask about the meaning of the word "acquired".
One final item I wish to speak to is item 69605-1. I have an idea that this item was the subject of debate in the last go-around on the Customs Tariff. It deals with scientific apparatus. My question is this: is this item' the answer to the incredible paper work burden that was to have been placed on universities and other charitable organizations which found themselves needing to import scientific apparatus?
Yes, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member is quite right. This was the subject matter of debate in the last budget and we think this now meets that concern.

Mr. Chairman, earlier I asked the minister whether he had made any studies of the effectiveness of duties on imported agricultural products relative to the effectiveness of duties in markets to which our agricultural products are shipped. Let me give the minister one example and then ask him a question. Unfortunately I have one sheet of figures missing but I think my Figures are roughly correct.
The tariff on peaches entering Canada was reduced from 18 per cent to 6.5 per cent over the last 25 years. Has the specific duty on a per pound basis remained constant? I believe the duty on canned peaches, for example, exported to the United States in dollars and cents terms has varied from 48 cents a case to $1.62 a case in the last 25 years. In view of the fact that the ad valorem duties applied by our major trading partner have become more effective in dollars and cents while ours have remained constant in dollars and cents but have declined in effectiveness, would the minister undertake a study to determine the impact upon agricultural production in Canada? We are using specific duties while markets to which we export are, in the main, using ad valorem or percentage rates on our products.

Mr. Chairman, as to whether a specific study will be undertaken, I think I can only go as far as saying that I will consider it. I point out that the Board has sought to deal with this problem, so far as peaches are concerned, under item 9211-1, which states that the MFN rate is three cents but not less than 121/2 per cent. So we have, if you like, placed a floor of an ad valorem rate underneath a specific duty.

In view of the fact that in 1950 Canada imported roughly 17V2 million pounds of peaches, while in 1975 we imported more than 101 million pounds of peaches, an increment of almost sixfold, and in view of the impact that this has on agriculture, would the minister treat this and other agricultural items as, for instance, penknives, pencils, and dozens of other miscellaneous items which do not create a major employment opportunity but are protected by duty, and give them comparable treatment? The minister has referred to negotiations which are going to take place in the Geneva talks. Would he approach former customers, present customers, and customers who have actually closed the doors on us, and determine whether or not we can have an equal trading
May 17, 1977

opportunity? I do not believe that agriculture is asking for anything more than an equal trading opportunity.
I think we are justified in asking for this and should have to pay a price. When we discuss duties with the United States we should tell the United States we would like an equal trading opportunity for products which we can produce, since we buy from them tens of millions of dollars worth of oranges, grapefruit, lemons, grapes, seed potatoes, and so on down the list. These are items which we cannot ship to them. I suggest our balance of trade in food items with the United States would be no more than fair were we to ask that duties be identical in effectiveness. They are reasonable, fair minded people, and I think this is a reasonable approach.

I would agree that it is, Mr. Chairman. We should, as I said earlier, seek to get reciprocity in these products, particularly where you have the example of the duty being higher than ours. With regard to the specific duty referred to, subject to confirmation I would say that would have been one which was bound under GATT as a result of the GATT negotiations in the late 1960's. In effect, we took the tariff system which existed then and at the same time bound those rates. We were not in a position to change them because they were international undertakings. As I said in my first response, the Tariff Board in its recommendation has sought to put agricultural products with ad valorem floors on the same basis as manufactured products.

We need the same basis as on those items we trade with the United States. We need comparable protection. Our farmers deserve it, as well as the manufacturers of pencils or the manufacturers of clothing.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-54, to amend the Excise Tax Act (No. 2), be read the second time and referred to the committee of the whole.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in the budget of May 25, 1976, I announced the government's intention to extend the air transportation tax to apply to an additional 2.3 million travellers who use Canadian airports annually. Although these air travellers make much the same use of Canadian facilities as taxable Canadian travellers, they do not currently pay the Canadian air transportation tax because they purchase their tickets outside Canada. Now, as a consequence of the amendments proposed in Bill C-54, they will be taxed in a manner which closely parallels that which applies to Canadians.
When first I announced the government's intention to extend this tax, I indicated that implementation would be preceded by consultation with interested parties to identify potential problems and difficulties. This process of consultation has now largely been completed, and it is proposed that the extension be made effective on November 1 of this year. This delay in coming into force will provide a necessary opportunity for the air carriers to make required alterations to their systems and procedures to implement the tax. As indicated in the ways and means motion, the tax will be extended to apply to any amount paid outside Canada for air transportation involving a departure from a Canadian airport for a destination outside Canada. This will ensure that all users of Canadian air facilities contribute in an equitable way to the upkeep of these facilities.
This bill also contains measures to change the current 12 per cent federal sales tax on gasoline and diesel fuel to an equivalent specific levy. The change is proposed in order to correct administrative and compliance difficulties which have existed for a number of years. The Excise Tax Act currently imposes a 12 per cent sales tax on the sale price of gasoline sold by manufacturers, and deems an importer of gasoline to be the manufacturer. Because of the nature of the petroleum industry, however, gasoline and diesel fuel are sold by manufacturers at a number of different levels of trade and at widely varying prices. The value for tax thus ranges from a very low level on inter-refinery sales to a relatively high level on sales to consumers through manufacturer's retail outlets.

May 17, 1977
Business of the House
In order to maintain a reasonable degree of equity and neutrality, Revenue Canada has allowed manufacturers to account for tax on all sales of gasoline and diesel fuel on the basis of weighted-average price determined periodically by Revenue Canada. The status of the resulting determined value is, however, uncertain under the law. I have therefore decided that, in recognition of the rather unique circumstances of this homogeneous product, and for greater certainty under the law, the statute should be amended to provide a series of specific levies to apply to the different grades of gasoline. The specific levies indicated in the motion and again in this bill are at the same rates which were put into effect by Revenue Canada on March 2, 1977.
The remainder of the bill deals with a series of relatively minor technical amendments designed to correct loopholes in existing provisions of the statute or to extend sales tax relief to certain users of products where a strong case for tax relief exists. In particular, the bill provides for the extension of the period within which a person may apply to recover tax by way of refund, deduction, or other payment, from two years to four years in the general refund provisions of the Excise Tax Act. This extension will apply to applications other than those which have expired on or before March 31, 1977.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, this bill seeks to implement the proposals contained in the ways and means motions of March 31 and April 18, 1977. With the exception of the extension of the air transportation tax, the proposed amendments are all relatively minor in nature, the emphasis being placed on correcting anomalies rather than making significant modifications in the scope or application of the federal sales tax. I would remind honourable members, however, that in conjunction with the budget, my colleague, the Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin), announced that the small manufacturer's regulation would be altered in such a way as to raise the exemption from sales tax which it provides from $3,000 to $10,000 of sales and to provide an exemption from sales tax on the products of certain Canadian craftsmen.
Hon. members will want to discuss the provisions of the bill in detail, and I will be glad to do so at committee stage.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-BRUCELLOSIS-POSSIBILITY OF RETURNING TO VACCINATION PROGRAM
AGRICULTURE-BRUCELLOSIS-POSSIBILITY OF RETURNING TO VACCINATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 4, 1977, as reported in Hansard at page 4594, I asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) about the situation regarding brucellosis and if he intended to return to vaccination. He said at that time that there has been a decrease in the number of affected cattle. Having looked up the statistics, I disagree with him, and I believe I can prove to him that some of the statistics he received were not up to date.
I am interested in the subject of vaccination for brucellosis. I ran a medical clinic, and we treated one of the early cases of undulant fever in a human being. That is a disease which can be contracted by human beings. They can be very sick or they can be chronically ill and still be working. It affects the bone. I remember one young veterinarian who contracted the disease. He had pain in his hip, and after we did a blood test the final diagnosis was that he had undulant fever with osteomyelitis. As I have said, in human beings it can cause very severe illness, and it can even be fatal. Of course some do not become so ill.
Back in 1953 brucellosis was running rampant, and many cows lost their calves through abortion. To overcome this, compulsory vaccination was adopted. That was commenced in 1956. This was carried out by the Health of Animals Branch of the Department of Agriculture without cost to the farmers. Reactors were shipped. Doubtfuls were re-tested. The stables were all disinfected and cleaned.
By 1964 the point was reached where some areas were able to be certified. This was in areas where only 5 per cent of the herds reacted and not more than one per cent of the animals were infected. With this very low incidence the disease appeared to be on the way out. Then the Brucellosis Act was introduced in 1965, and that terminated compulsory vaccination. Both the provincial governments and the federal government were involved in that act. From that date on fewer calves were vaccinated. In other words, vaccination of calves was discouraged because of the markets in some areas where calves were being shipped. Some calves were sold as cows and some of them would occasionally react, so some countries did not want to buy them. From that date on fewer calves were vaccinated.
From 1969 to 1973 it appeared that the disease was remaining under control, and there was a false sense of security. In 1969, for instance, 211 herds were affected. In 1972, 209 herds were affected. Both levels of government were in favour of the
May 17, 1977

eradication program which de-emphasized vaccination. During this period of time compensation paid for the animals which were destroyed was rightfully increased when they had to be shipped.
The federal government kept supplying the vaccine, and some of the good dairy farmers kept vaccinating, but of course they then had to pay for the vaccine. In 1953 when this plan was started, we were vaccinating 400,000 calves per year, and the Health of Animals Branch was paying the cost of this. However, all at once outbreaks started to recur, and here in eastern Ontario we probably had the first outbreak. Then there were other minor outbreaks. These were more insolated cases occurring in western Ontario. So at the end of 1973, 48 herds were removed. In 1973 there were 1,038 reactors. It is interesting to note that in 1974 there were 337 herds under quarantine, an increase of over eight times in the space of one year. The reactors, from January 1 to September 30 of that year, were 3,168, a ten times increase. Therefore the evidence shows that we have a return of a disaster that we thought we had conquered. Instead of that, from January to March of this year there have been 50 newly infected herds found. Multiply that by six and you get 300 new herds per year.
I would point out to the minister that this sort of thing has happened in the field of human medicine. We stopped vaccination and had to go back to it. I believe that we have to return to vaccination in Ontario and the rest of Canada. There has been a division of opinion between the Ontario government and the federal government. The Ontario government believes we should return to vaccination but the federal government does not.
